egm-101.question: A 79-year-old woman has a Medtronic dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for sinus node dysfunction, programmed AAIR<=>DDDR (MVP), with known first-degree AV block. Routine transmission, no symptoms. How do you interpret this recording?
options: Ventricular undersensing: a spontaneous QRS was missed
Normal MVP function (non-conducted P wave tolerated)
Intermittent loss of ventricular capture; check the threshold
Permanent switch to DDDR after complete AV block was detected
commentaires: Incorrect: no QRS appears on the RV EGM or the far-field EGM after the 4th P wave, so there is nothing to sense.
Correct: the non-conducted P wave is followed by no ventricular event; the device delivers a backup pace 80 ms after the next AS, hence the V-V pause of about 1550 ms.
Incorrect: the only ventricular spike (VP) is followed by a broad evoked response on both ventricular channels.
Incorrect: AS-VS conduction resumes from the next cycle with a long PR interval; a single blocked P wave is not enough to make MVP switch.
egm-101.explication: In "monitored" AAI(R), MVP allows intrinsic conduction even when it is slow (here PR ≈ 240 ms). When a P wave is followed by no ventricular event, the device does not pace in the same cycle: it delivers a ventricular backup pace 80 ms after the next atrial event. The marker channel thus shows AS without VS, then AS–VP at 80 ms and a V-V interval of ≈ 1550 ms. This is the expected behaviour, not a malfunction. Switching to DDD(R) only occurs if loss of conduction recurs (2 of the last 4 A-A intervals).
egm-101.aRetenir: MVP: an isolated blocked P wave is tolerated, and the ventricular backup pace comes 80 ms after the next P wave; the resulting pause is normal.

egm-102.question: A 68-year-old man has a Medtronic dual-chamber ICD (secondary prevention, ischaemic cardiomyopathy) programmed to MVP. He has had two episodes of polymorphic VT, each starting just after a sequence similar to the one on this EGM. Which statements are correct?
options: The blocked P wave creates a short–long–short sequence that can promote pause-dependent VT
Programming DDD(R) mode with an appropriate AV delay is a reasonable option in this patient
The observed pause is abnormal and requires replacement of the ventricular lead
A second blocked P wave within the next 4 A-A intervals would switch the device to DDD(R)
MVP paces the ventricle in the same cycle as the blocked P wave, which prevents any pause
commentaires: Correct: a short cycle (PVC or preceding cycle), a pause due to the blocked P wave, then the next beat: this is the proarrhythmic pattern described in ICD recipients.
Correct: in a patient with pause-dependent VT, eliminating pauses (DDD(R), possibly with a higher lower rate) takes priority over minimising RV pacing.
Incorrect: the pause results from the algorithm; the lead is working normally.
Correct: loss of conduction in 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals triggers the switch to DDD(R), followed by periodic conduction checks.
Incorrect: the backup pace is only delivered after the next atrial event, which is precisely what creates the pause.
egm-102.explication: MVP accepts a non-conducted P wave and only paces the ventricle in the next cycle (80 ms after the AS), which produces a pause. In some ICD recipients, the resulting short–long–short sequence has been associated with pause-dependent VT. When such a relationship is documented, DDD(R) mode (with a long AV delay or a conduction search algorithm) is preferred over MVP. The device switches to DDD(R) on its own if loss of conduction affects 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals, but then returns to AAI(R) after a successful conduction check.
egm-102.aRetenir: VT triggered after a blocked P wave in MVP: think short–long–short and prefer DDD(R) mode.

egm-103.question: An 83-year-old man with complete AV block has a dual-chamber pacemaker with beat-to-beat ventricular capture verification (AutoCapture type); output amplitude is set just above the measured threshold. The GP, who receives the remote monitoring report, is worried about "loss of capture" in this pacemaker-dependent patient. Based on this EGM, how do you reply?
options: Risk of asystole: the ventricular lead must be revised
Expected behaviour: each loss of capture is backed up
Capture verification should be disabled and output fixed at 5 V
This is crosstalk corrected by safety pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: each VP without an evoked response is followed about 100 ms later by a backup pulse that captures; no pause occurs.
Correct: the algorithm recognised the absence of an evoked response and delivered a high-output backup pulse, which captures; isolated events are expected with an output close to threshold.
Incorrect: this would reduce longevity with no benefit; safety is ensured by the backup pulse, and the threshold is automatically remeasured if losses recur.

Incorrect: safety pacing follows sensing in the crosstalk window after an AP; here the P wave is sensed (AS) and it is the absence of an evoked response to the first VP that triggers the second pulse.
egm-103.explication: Beat-to-beat capture verification algorithms analyse the evoked response after each ventricular pulse. If none is detected, they deliver a high-output backup pulse within ~100 ms: on the EGM, the first spike is followed by no depolarisation, the second one is, and the dependent patient has no pause. This is what allows the output to be set close to threshold, to the benefit of longevity. Repeated loss of capture triggers a new threshold measurement and an amplitude adjustment. Isolated backup pulses are therefore expected and reassuring; if they become frequent, the threshold and lead should be checked, and fusion, which would distort evoked response analysis, looked for.
egm-103.aRetenir: Isolated backup pulses with beat-to-beat capture verification: expected behaviour that protects the dependent patient; only a concern if they become frequent.

egm-104.question: Dual-chamber ICD recipient (ischaemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 30%). VT zone 150–188 bpm with ATP, VF zone > 188 bpm (cycle length < 320 ms) with ATP during charging then shocks. Remote monitoring alert. Which reading is correct?
options: VT at 360 ms terminated by ATP, then return to sinus rhythm
Poorly discriminated sinus tachycardia, misclassified as VT by the device
VT at 360 ms accelerated by ATP to ≈ 235 ms (VF zone), charging
RV lead noise triggering false VF detection
commentaires: Incorrect: after the TP burst, the tachycardia persists with shorter cycles; there is no return to sinus rhythm.
Incorrect: the ventricle is beating at 360 ms, dissociated from the atrium, which remains at 800 ms (V > A): this is VT.
Correct: cycles go from 360 ms to ≈ 230–250 ms with a new morphology; they fall in the VF zone (FS) and the device charges.
Incorrect: the rapid signals are organised depolarisations, also visible on the shock EGM; this is not non-physiological noise confined to the RV EGM.
egm-104.explication: The initial VT is monomorphic at 360 ms, with V > A dissociation (sinus atrial rhythm at 800 ms). The ATP burst at 88% (≈ 317 ms) does not terminate it: it converts it into a faster tachycardia (≈ 235 ms) with a different morphology, classified in the VF zone (FS) and followed by charging. Acceleration by ATP is rare but well recognised, which is why a shock must always be programmed after any ATP therapy. After such an episode, a trigger should be sought, and ATP adjustment and long-term treatment (antiarrhythmic drug, ablation) discussed.
egm-104.aRetenir: Cycles that shorten and change morphology after ATP: VT acceleration, taken over by the VF zone and a shock.

egm-105.question: A 72-year-old man has a dual-chamber ICD with the VT detection zone programmed at 150 bpm (400 ms). He presents with 2 days of dyspnoea and palpitations; the device has recorded no treated episode. You start a real-time EGM. What is the interpretation?
options: Sinus tachycardia at 120 bpm, 1:1 conduction
VT at 120 bpm, below the VT zone cut-off
Undetected atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
Harmless slow idioventricular rhythm
commentaires: Incorrect: the P waves remain at 800 ms while the ventricle beats at 500 ms (V > A); there is no 1:1 relationship.
Correct: the ventricle beats regularly at 500 ms (120 bpm), faster than the atrium and with a different morphology on the shock EGM; at 500 ms, it stays above the 400 ms cut-off and is not detected.
Incorrect: atrial activity is slow and regular (800 ms), with no rapid flutter waves.
Incorrect: 120 bpm is well above the rate of an idioventricular rhythm, and the patient is symptomatic.
egm-105.explication: The marker channel shows only VS: the device sees every beat but, at 500 ms, none falls in the VT zone (< 400 ms), so there is no detection or therapy. The EGMs show a ventricle faster than the atrium (V > A, dissociation) with a change in morphology compared with the first two conducted beats: this is slow VT, common on antiarrhythmic drugs or in advanced heart disease. Management combines treatment of the episode (manual ATP, cardioversion) and, if the slow VT recurs, a detection zone programmed about 10 bpm below its rate, with discriminators enabled.
egm-105.aRetenir: Regular VS markers and V > A in a symptomatic ICD recipient: think slow VT below the detection zone.

egm-106.question: Dual-chamber ICD, VT zone from 150 bpm (400 ms) with discriminators enabled. Episode stored as "SVT — therapy withheld". What reasoning led the device to withhold therapy?
options: Atrial rate is twice the ventricular rate (A > V)
The ventricular rate is irregular, suggesting AF
The onset was gradual, in keeping with sinus tachycardia
The ventricular cycles are below the VT zone cut-off
commentaires: Correct: the atrium beats at 190 ms and the ventricle at 380 ms; an atrial rate higher than the ventricular rate points to a tachycardia of atrial origin.
Incorrect: the V-V intervals are perfectly regular at 380 ms.
Incorrect: the change from 833 to 380 ms is abrupt, not the gradual acceleration of sinus tachycardia.
Incorrect: 380 ms is shorter than 400 ms, so the cycles are correctly classified as TS in the VT zone.
egm-106.explication: After two sinus beats, the atrial EGM shows regular activity at 190 ms, every other wave of which is conducted (AS) while the other falls just after the QRS (AR). The ventricle, with a morphology identical to sinus rhythm, beats at 380 ms, in the VT zone. The A/V discriminator finds A > V with a fixed (2:1) relationship: it withholds therapy and classifies the episode as SVT (atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia with 2:1 conduction). Further management is that of the atrial arrhythmia: anticoagulation according to the CHA2DS2-VA score, rate control and discussion of ablation.
egm-106.aRetenir: Regular A > V (2:1) with QRS identical to sinus rhythm: conducted atrial tachycardia, therapy rightly withheld.

egm-107.question: Dual-chamber ICD in a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy. Episode recorded during palpitations. Which features of this tracing point to VT rather than supraventricular tachycardia?
options: The first beat of the tachycardia is ventricular, and the atrium follows
The shock EGM morphology differs from that of the sinus beats
An A/V ratio of 1
The perfect regularity of the cycles
The abrupt onset of the tachycardia
commentaires: Correct: the tachycardia starts with a premature ventricular event (470 ms after the last VS), and each atrial event follows the ventricle by ≈ 170 ms.
Correct: on the shock (far-field) EGM, the tachycardia QRS is broad and different from the sinus QRS: this is the basis of morphology algorithms.
Incorrect: a 1:1 ratio is seen in SVT as well as in VT with retrograde conduction; it does not discriminate.
Incorrect: VT and SVT (AVNRT, reciprocating tachycardia) are both regular.
Correct: abrupt onset rules out sinus tachycardia, without on its own distinguishing VT from other SVTs.
egm-107.explication: 1:1 tachycardias are the hardest to discriminate. Here several arguments converge: the mode of onset (first event ventricular, atrium "lagging behind" with a fixed V-A interval of ≈ 170 ms), the abrupt onset and, above all, the change in morphology on the shock EGM compared with sinus rhythm. The A/V ratio and regularity do not settle the question. Dual-chamber devices combine these criteria (morphology, onset, A-V timing); when in doubt, the default programming favours therapy.
egm-107.aRetenir: 1:1 tachycardia: ventricular onset and a change in morphology point to VT; the 1:1 ratio and regularity do not discriminate.

egm-108.question: A 76-year-old man with a dual-chamber ICD (single-coil RV lead) and chronic kidney disease on an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone is admitted with dehydration: potassium 7.4 mmol/l, QRS widened to 180 ms. He receives a shock on waking. Here is the EGM stored before detection. What is the mechanism?
options: T-wave oversensing, 300 ms after each QRS
Ventricular fibrillation with short, irregular cycles
Double counting of the widened QRS
P-wave oversensing by a malpositioned RV lead
commentaires: Incorrect: the second marker occurs ≈ 150 ms after the VS, still within the broad QRS, not at the time of the T wave (~300 ms).
Incorrect: the shock EGM shows organised sinus rhythm at ≈ 830 ms; the intervals alternate 150/680 ms.
Correct: on the RV EGM, the widened QRS has a second deflection that extends beyond the end of the post-sense blanking period and is counted a second time (FS).
Incorrect: the P waves are visible on the atrial EGM, offset in time; the second V signal is attached to each QRS.
egm-108.explication: A very broad QRS (hyperkalaemia, class I antiarrhythmic drug, CRT with an RV–LV delay) can extend beyond the blanking period following ventricular sensing: its late component is then sensed as a new event. The marker channel shows alternating very short (≈ 150 ms) and long intervals, which doubles the counted rate and may lead to inappropriate therapy. It is distinguished from T-wave oversensing by its timing (within the QRS, not ~300 ms later). Treatment: correct the cause (here hyperkalaemia) and, if needed, lengthen the post-sense blanking period or reduce sensitivity where the device allows.
egm-108.aRetenir: Alternating ≈ 150 ms / long intervals with a broad QRS: QRS double counting, think hyperkalaemia.

egm-109.question: An episode of "untreated VF — non-sustained" is transmitted from a dual-chamber ICD. The patient says he was using an angle grinder in his workshop at the time of the episode. What is your interpretation and management?
options: RV lead fracture: schedule surgical lead revision
Self-terminating VF: increase the beta-blocker
External interference: identify the source, no lead revision
Pectoral myopotential oversensing: reduce the sensitivity
commentaires: Incorrect: lead noise affects only the channel of the faulty lead; here all three channels are contaminated simultaneously.
Incorrect: the signal is high-frequency and regular, unlike VF, and the sinus QRS complexes remain visible through it.
Correct: a fixed-frequency artefact, simultaneous on the A EGM, RV EGM and shock EGM, starting and stopping abruptly, indicates an external electromagnetic source.
Incorrect: myopotentials are irregular, related to arm effort, and predominate on vectors including the can (shock EGM, unipolar configurations), not on intracardiac bipoles.
egm-109.explication: Electromagnetic interference is recognised by a high-frequency signal of regular appearance, present simultaneously on all channels (including the atrial and ventricular bipoles, which share no conductor), with an abrupt onset and offset corresponding to the use of an appliance. The spontaneous QRS complexes remain visible through it. The device counted it as rapid activity (AS/AR, FS), hence the stored episode. No lead revision is warranted: identify the source (faulty tool, poor earthing, proximity), advise keeping a sufficient distance and check that the lead parameters are normal.
egm-109.aRetenir: Artefact simultaneous on all channels = external source; noise confined to one channel = lead.

egm-110.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker implanted 6 years ago for AV block. Over the past 3 weeks, remote monitoring has reported dozens of short "AT/AF" episodes with mode switching; atrial impedance has risen from 480 to 1900 Ω. Here is one episode. What do you do?
options: Start anticoagulation after calculating the CHA2DS2-VA score
Increase atrial sensitivity to detect AF more reliably
Start an antiarrhythmic drug to reduce the AF burden
Suspect an atrial lead problem and check the lead
commentaires: Incorrect: the "episodes" consist of non-physiological signals; the underlying rhythm is sinus, and there is no AF to anticoagulate.
Incorrect: increasing sensitivity would make noise sensing worse.
Incorrect: there is no atrial arrhythmia to treat.
Correct: bursts of irregular spikes at intervals < 100 ms on the A EGM only, sinus P waves visible between bursts, and an abrupt rise in impedance: an atrial lead fault is likely.
egm-110.explication: On the atrial EGM, bursts of very brief signals of variable amplitude and non-physiological intervals (< 100 ms) appear intermittently, while sinus P waves remain visible and the ventricular EGM is normal. The device interprets them as AF and mode switches (MS). The abrupt rise in impedance confirms a conductor problem. This should be checked in clinic (measurements, provocative manoeuvres of the arm and pocket, chest X-ray), with reprogramming if needed (non-atrial-tracking mode) before revision. False episodes must be excluded from the AF burden: no anticoagulation decision should be made without reviewing the EGMs.
egm-110.aRetenir: Non-physiological bursts on the A EGM alone + rising impedance: false AF due to an atrial lead fault, no anticoagulation.

egm-111.question: "Shock delivered" alert in a 64-year-old man with a primary prevention ICD. Programmed shocks: first shock at 25 J, subsequent ones at maximum energy. Which reading of the episode is correct?
options: A single successful shock, followed by bradycardia pacing
Two shocks for monomorphic VT, the first having accelerated the VT
Two shocks delivered for lead noise, with no real arrhythmia
VF: first shock unsuccessful, second shock successful
commentaires: Incorrect: after the first shock (CD), fibrillatory activity persists and a new charge is needed.
Incorrect: ventricular activity is disorganised (FS at 170–240 ms, variable amplitude) from the outset: this is VF.
Incorrect: the disorganised activity is visible on the RV EGM and the shock EGM, and the rhythm returns after the second shock.
Correct: FS, charging, first shock without effect, redetection and second charge, then a second shock followed by pacing (VP).
egm-111.explication: The tracing shows detected VF (FS), charging (Chg), a first shock (CD) after which fibrillation persists, redetection, a new charge and a successful second shock, followed by post-shock bradycardia pacing. An unsuccessful first shock at reduced energy should prompt programming all shocks at maximum energy (as recommended by the programming consensus), followed by a search for a cause: shock impedance, antiarrhythmic drug (amiodarone), electrolyte disturbance, ischaemia, progression of heart disease, and consideration of the shock vector or polarity.
egm-111.aRetenir: An unsuccessful shock for VF: program all shocks at maximum energy and look for the cause.

egm-112.question: CRT-D in a 70-year-old woman (LVEF 28%, LBBB): worsening dyspnoea, alert "biventricular pacing 81%". Persistent AF for 5 weeks, mean rate 95 bpm on a beta-blocker. Which management options are appropriate?
options: Discuss a rhythm control strategy (cardioversion, AF ablation)
Lower the lower rate to allow intrinsic conduction to emerge
Consider AV junction ablation if BiV pacing remains insufficient
Rely on VS-triggered pacing algorithms to restore resynchronisation
commentaires: Correct: restoring sinus rhythm re-establishes AV synchrony and BiV pacing; this is an option in a symptomatic patient with recent-onset AF.
Incorrect: this would further increase the proportion of intrinsic conduction, the opposite of the goal.
Correct: the 2021 ESC guidelines support AV junction ablation (IIa) in AF patients whose BiV pacing remains incomplete despite treatment.
Incorrect: pacing triggered after sensing mainly produces fusion or pseudo-fusion beats, without true resynchronisation.
egm-112.explication: On the EGM, AF is conducted rapidly and irregularly: most cycles are VS with an intrinsic QRS, and BiV pacing only occurs after the longest cycles. The BiV percentage falls, whereas at least 98% is the target to obtain the benefit of CRT. The pacing counter often overestimates true BiV capture, as it includes fusion beats. Management combines optimisation of rate control, a rhythm control strategy where feasible and, if this fails, AV junction ablation to achieve 100% BiV pacing.
egm-112.aRetenir: CRT with conducted AF: insufficient %BiV; control rhythm or rate, or even ablate the AV junction.

egm-113.question: Single-chamber VVI pacemaker, lower rate 60 bpm, in an 88-year-old woman with slow permanent AF. The remote monitoring nurse flags a "pause" on this recording that is longer than the lower rate interval. How do you explain it?
options: Undersensing of the QRS preceding the pause
Rate hysteresis programmed at 50 bpm
Sleep function lowering the lower rate
T-wave oversensing prolonging the escape interval
commentaires: Incorrect: each spontaneous QRS is marked VS; sensing is correct.
Correct: after a sensed event, the escape interval is that of the hysteresis rate (1200 ms = 50 bpm); once pacing is established, the device paces at the lower rate (1000 ms = 60 bpm).
Incorrect: a sleep rate would also change the interval between two paced beats, which remains at 1000 ms here.
Incorrect: no intermediate sensed event appears on the marker channel during the pause.
egm-113.explication: Rate hysteresis lengthens the escape interval after a spontaneous beat to allow the patient's own rhythm to emerge. Here, the last VS is followed by an escape interval of 1200 ms (50 bpm), then pacing continues at the lower rate (1000 ms). When the spontaneous rhythm returns at a faster rate (750 ms), the device is inhibited. An apparent pause longer than the lower rate interval is therefore not a malfunction: the programmed settings must be known before diagnosing oversensing.
egm-113.aRetenir: Escape interval longer than the lower rate after a VS, then pacing at the lower rate: hysteresis.

egm-114.question: An implantable loop recorder was inserted after a cryptogenic ischaemic stroke. A 4-hour "AF" episode is transmitted. Which features of the tracing allow the physician to confirm the episode as genuine AF?
options: Irregularly irregular RR intervals, with no repeating pattern
Absence of organised P waves before the QRS complexes
The "AF" label assigned by the device
A fibrillatory baseline between the QRS complexes
A ventricular rate above 100 bpm
commentaires: Correct: the intervals vary from 440 to 930 ms with no grouping or alternation, unlike frequent PACs.
Correct: no P wave precedes the QRS complexes, whereas they are visible in false positives due to PACs.
Incorrect: the algorithm is wrong in a substantial proportion of cases (PACs, noise, undersensing); every detection must be reviewed.
Correct: the irregular undulation of the baseline reflects fibrillatory atrial activity.
Incorrect: AF may be slow or have a normal rate; the rate does not make the diagnosis.
egm-114.explication: Implantable loop recorders detect AF from RR irregularity (and sometimes the absence of P waves), with an imperfect positive predictive value: PACs, noise and undersensing generate false episodes. The physician must review the subcutaneous ECG. Here, the RR intervals are irregularly irregular, no P wave precedes the QRS complexes and the baseline is fibrillatory: this is genuine AF. In a patient who has had a stroke, its confirmation leads to a discussion of anticoagulation according to the 2024 ESC guidelines.
egm-114.aRetenir: AF on an implantable loop recorder: irregularly irregular RR, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline; always review the EGM before deciding.

egm-115.question: DDD dual-chamber pacemaker, lower rate 60 bpm, paced AV delay 250 ms, intact intrinsic AV conduction (sinus node dysfunction). Check 3 weeks after implantation. What is the abnormality?
options: Intermittent loss of atrial capture
Intermittent loss of ventricular capture
Atrial undersensing with competitive pacing
Crosstalk with inhibition of ventricular pacing
commentaires: Correct: on some cycles, the AP spike is followed by no P wave; without atrial activation, nothing is conducted and the device paces the ventricle at the end of the AV delay (VP at 250 ms).
Incorrect: each VP is followed by a broad evoked response on the RV EGM and the far-field EGM.
Incorrect: no spontaneous P wave is visible; all atrial events are paced.
Incorrect: the ventricle is paced (VP), not inhibited; there is no early V sensing after AP.
egm-115.explication: When the atrial pulse captures, the atrium depolarises and the impulse is conducted: VS at ≈ 200 ms. On three cycles, the atrial spike is followed by no P wave on the atrial EGM: there is nothing to conduct and the ventricle is paced at the end of the programmed AV delay (250 ms), with a different, paced QRS. Early after implantation, this suggests atrial lead dislodgement or a rise in threshold. Measure the atrial threshold, increase the amplitude with an adequate safety margin and check the lead position (chest X-ray).
egm-115.aRetenir: AP not followed by a P wave, then VP at the end of the AV delay in a patient who conducts: loss of atrial capture.

egm-116.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction with normal AV conduction (PR 180–240 ms). Sensed AV delay programmed at 200 ms, with no conduction-preserving algorithm. Ventricular pacing percentage displayed: 78%. On several cycles, the ventricular spike falls within a spontaneous QRS whose appearance is unchanged. How do you interpret these cycles?
options: Intermittent loss of capture: increase ventricular output
Ventricular undersensing: spontaneous QRS complexes are missed
Pseudo-fusion: ineffective spikes, wrongly counted as pacing
True fusion: hybrid QRS, partly paced and partly intrinsic
commentaires: Incorrect: capture is not the issue; the spike falls on myocardium already activated by intrinsic conduction, so it cannot capture.
Incorrect: the QRS is not missed; its activation simply has not yet reached the RV lead when the AV delay expires.
Correct: the spike, delivered once the spontaneous QRS is already under way, does not alter activation; the device nevertheless counts it as pacing, hence a misleading VP percentage.
Incorrect: true fusion produces a QRS of intermediate morphology; here the appearance is that of the spontaneous QRS.
egm-116.explication: The intrinsic PR interval fluctuates around the programmed AV delay: depending on the cycle, the QRS is sensed (VS), paced, or a spike falls within a spontaneous QRS already under way without altering its appearance (pseudo-fusion). The spike is delivered because intrinsic activation has not yet reached the RV lead by the end of the AV delay; it falls in the refractory period and has no effect. The device nevertheless counts these pseudo-fusion beats as paced, hence a misleading VP percentage, which should lead to a conclusion of neither pacemaker dependence nor loss of capture. Management is to promote intrinsic conduction with a conduction-preserving algorithm (AV hysteresis, conduction search, AAI/DDD switching modes), since unnecessary RV pacing is harmful in the long term.
egm-116.aRetenir: V spike within a spontaneous QRS of unchanged appearance: pseudo-fusion, ineffective but counted as VP, which inflates the pacing percentage.

egm-117.question: A 47-year-old electrician has a dual-chamber ICD for primary prevention (dilated cardiomyopathy). An episode was recorded at his workplace, with no therapy delivered. True or false: had this phenomenon lasted a few seconds longer, the device could have delivered an inappropriate shock.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: the artefact is counted as very short intervals (FS); if it persists beyond the VF zone detection duration, the device charges and may deliver a shock.
Incorrect: SVT–VT discriminators do not apply in the VF zone, and an artefact also present on the shock EGM defeats lead noise algorithms.
egm-117.explication: The regular, high-frequency artefact appears simultaneously on the A EGM, RV EGM and shock EGM, with an abrupt onset and offset: this is external electromagnetic interference. The device counts it as very rapid ventricular activity (FS); the episode, which was brief (about 3 seconds), did not meet the programmed duration criterion. Longer exposure (arc welding station, faulty tool, high-current conductor) may meet it and lead to charging followed by an inappropriate shock: in the VF zone, discriminators do not apply, and noise algorithms that compare the RV EGM with a far-field EGM are defeated when the latter is also contaminated. In an exposed worker, the workplace should be assessed (distance, earthing, field measurements with the occupational health service or the manufacturer), and the patient taught to move away from the source at the slightest symptom.
egm-117.aRetenir: Prolonged electromagnetic interference is counted as VF and may lead to an inappropriate shock; assess occupational exposure.

egm-118.question: A 64-year-old woman with cardiac sarcoidosis on amiodarone has a dual-chamber ICD with a VT zone from 150 bpm. She presents with 6 hours of palpitations; she is conscious, BP 105/70 mmHg. Real-time EGM on the programmer. True or false: an immediate attempt can be made to terminate this rhythm with ATP delivered manually from the programmer, under ECG monitoring with an external defibrillator at hand.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: all ICDs allow manually commanded ATP (burst or ramp) or shocks to be delivered from the programmer; for well-tolerated slow VT, manual ATP is often effective and painless.
Incorrect: VT below the detection zone can still be treated with a manually commanded therapy; external cardioversion is not the first resort in a stable patient.
egm-118.explication: The EGM shows slow ventricular tachycardia (regular cycles of 500 ms, i.e. 120 bpm), dissociated from the atria and with a morphology different from the sinus beats: it remains below the VT zone cut-off (400 ms), hence no automatic therapy. In a conscious, stable patient, the programmer allows manual ATP to be delivered immediately (burst at about 81–88% of the cycle length). Like any ATP, it may accelerate the VT: work under ECG monitoring with an external defibrillator ready, with a commanded internal shock or external cardioversion under sedation as fallbacks. Then look for a cause (ischaemia, potassium, amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction, sarcoidosis flare), program a detection zone about 10 bpm below the rate of this slow VT with discriminators enabled, and discuss ablation if it recurs.
egm-118.aRetenir: Slow VT below the zone in a stable ICD recipient: manual ATP from the programmer, external defibrillator ready, then an adjusted zone.
